Could a Job Guarantee Mitigate Mass AI Unemployment? Economists and Lawmakers Weigh Proposals

29 Oct 2026, 06:32 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Tech Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

3 min read

Key takeawaysAs artificial intelligence rapidly advances, technology leaders and economists are increasingly warning about potential widespread job displacement across white-collar and technical professions. In response, policymakers and researchers are revisiting an old economic concept: the federal job guarantee.

As artificial intelligence rapidly advances, technology leaders and economists are increasingly warning about potential widespread job displacement across white-collar and technical professions. In response, policymakers and researchers are revisiting an old economic concept: the federal job guarantee.

Prominent figures have raised alarms about the employment timeline for AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, affecting fields such as law, technology, and finance. Similarly, Bill Gates has predicted that AI will advance swiftly enough to reduce the need for human labor for most tasks within a decade. Observers note that even if these labor-market predictions do not materialize exactly as forecasted, a collapse in heavily backed AI investments could spark broader economic recessions.

Exploring the Job Guarantee Model

To counter potential mass joblessness, advocates are championing the job guarantee—a public option ensuring that anyone wanting work can secure a meaningful, decently paid position. Proponents argue this approach shields individuals from the psychological and financial toll of unemployment while addressing societal needs like climate adaptation, infrastructure, elder care, and childcare.

The concept draws on historical precedents, such as Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Works Progress Administration (WPA) during the Great Depression, as well as modern implementations in countries like France, India, and Argentina. Proponents also cite polling indicating stronger public support for job guarantees compared to universal basic income (UBI), emphasizing that employment offers community connection, skill development, and dignity beyond mere financial support.

Legislative Proposals and Taxation Ideas

In the United States, policymakers have introduced legislative measures related to the concept:

  • Congressional Resolution: US Representative Ayanna Pressley reintroduced a resolution calling for a federally funded, locally administered job guarantee paying at least $25 an hour, adjusted for the cost of living. The proposal focuses on sectors like disaster relief, child and senior care, and public art projects.
  • AI Token and Revenue Tax: Representatives Greg Casar, Valerie Foushee, and Sara Jacobs proposed taxing large artificial intelligence companies based on their token volume or product revenue to fund a federal job guarantee, with tax rates scaling up if unemployment rises.
  • Private-Sector Wage Subsidies: In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) launched a pilot program subsidizing wages for van drivers to reach an "autonomous wage" threshold, aiming to help workers exit safety-net benefit dependencies while lowering labor costs for employers.

Cost Calculations and Political Debate

The financial feasibility of a federal job guarantee remains a subject of intense debate. Critics, such as Republican Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, have argued during congressional hearings that such programs would cost trillions of dollars and remain practically unachievable.

Conversely, economists argue that traditional cost tallies overlook systemic savings. Oxford economics professor Max Kasy noted that job guarantees offset government expenditures by reducing unemployment, disability, and early retirement payouts while generating new tax revenues and social insurance contributions. Bard College economics professor Pavlina Tcherneva added that accounting for the health costs tied to precarious long-term unemployment makes such investments economically viable.

Practical Implications and Reader Verification

Readers evaluating economic policy proposals and labor-market trends should consider several confirmed details alongside open questions:

  • What is confirmed: Industry leaders have issued warnings regarding potential white-collar AI displacement; lawmakers have introduced specific congressional resolutions and tax proposals in the US; and small-scale pilot programs like the one in Cleveland are actively testing wage subsidies.
  • What remains unknown: Whether large-scale AI unemployment will actually occur on predicted timelines, how much a federal job guarantee would ultimately cost taxpayers on a national scale, and whether bipartisan consensus can be reached for implementation.
  • How to verify: Readers can review original legislative filings via congressional tracking websites, read official statements from lawmakers such as Representative Ayanna Pressley and Representative Greg Casar, and consult economic research papers published by academic institutions like Oxford University and Bard College.

For the original report and full contextual details, readers can consult the coverage published by The Guardian.
